beats.text: Twelve custom chips for one calculator.
beats.note: In April 1969, Japanese calculator company Busicom asked Intel to build a twelve chip set, according to Intel's own history page.
One of them could be programmed. Ted Hoff and Stanley Mazor wrote the specifications, says IEEE Spectrum.

beats.name: Federico Faggin
beats.role: Hired in April 1970. Took over design leadership from Hoff, with Masatoshi Shima of Busicom checking the logic.

beats.note: It held exclusive rights, so Intel could not sell the 4004 to anyone else.

beats.context: Intel says CEO Robert Noyce repurchased the rights, for everything but calculators, in May 1971 by returning Busicom's $60,000 investment. IEEE and Wikipedia describe a price break instead.

beats.text: Announcing a new era of integrated electronics.
beats.note: Intel began advertising the 4004 in November 1971. Wikipedia dates the announcement to 15 November, in Electronic News.

beats.text: The microprocessor was a calculator job. Selling it to the world was the renegotiation.
